content: Breast pain, also known as mastalgia, is a frequently encountered symptom in general surgical practice. Breast discharge, on the other hand, is rarely considered normal except in cases of lactating or pregnant women. Differential Diagnosis Breast Discharge Breast discharge can be associated with a variety of conditions, including: Breast abscess Breast cancer Chronic nipple stimulation Cirrhosis or other hepatic diseases Duct ectasia Early pregnancy Fibroadenosis Fibrocystic changes Galactorrhea Hypothalamic and pituitary abnormalities Hypothyroidism Intraductal papilloma Lactation Lactorrhoea Late pregnancy Medications Mondor's disease Paget's disease of the nipple Prolactinoma Puberty Pseudocyesis Retroareolar abscess Sarcoidosis Systemic lupus erythematosus Tuberculosis Breast Pain Breast pain may arise from a range of causes, including: Breast abscess Breast cancer Cyclical mastalgia Cysts Duct ectasia Extramammary causes of pain Fat necrosis Fibroadenoma Fibrocystic changes Herpes zoster Intraductal papilloma Lactation Lipoma Mastitis Mondor's disease Non-cyclical mastalgia Pregnancy Phyllodes tumor Rib secondaries Tietze's disease Trauma Unilateral or bilateral gynecomastia Diagnosis History and Symptoms A thorough history should be obtained, including: Family history of breast or other relevant diseases Menstrual history Pregnancy history Physical Examination Assess the pattern and duration of pain and/or discharge. Perform a complete breast examination, ideally after the menstrual flow has ended (at least 7–9 days post-menstruation). Laboratory Findings The following laboratory tests may be useful in the diagnostic workup: Complete blood count (CBC) Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) Liver function tests (LFTs) Prolactin levels Serum calcium levels Beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) Luteinizing hormone (LH) Chest X-Ray A chest x-ray may be indicated to rule out secondary involvement of the lungs or ribs.
